payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make her close her jacket fully
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: In the edited image, is the woman's jacket fully closed, with its front panels together and no visible opening remaining along the closure?
node.criteria: Pass: the jacket is visibly fully closed, with its front panels together and no opening along the closure. Fail: the jacket is visibly not fully closed, including any visible opening along the closure. Unknown: the closure or its full extent cannot be judged from the image.
node.binding: Directly inspect the requested endpoint in the edited image; the input image is context for identifying the woman's jacket, not a prerequisite for checking the endpoint.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image shows the woman's jacket hanging open, with a clear gap between the front panels.
The edited image shows the jacket hanging open, with a clear gap between its front panels.
The jacket is visibly open in the edited image, with its front panels separated and a large opening remaining.
The jacket is visibly open in the edited image, with its front panels separated and a large opening remaining.
The edited image shows the jacket hanging open, with a clear gap between its front panels.

fulfillment: The node’s closure criterion and dependency logic are already explicit, and the repeated traces consistently report an open jacket with no visible progress. But the attached edited image appears to show the woman turned sideways with the bright pink jacket wrapped or brought across her front; the closure line is partly obscured by her pose and the garment’s drape. This is a visual-evidence disagreement, not a transport, schema, or dependency failure: all checks are valid and queried, with no execution errors. Improve the binding/decision procedure to inspect the jacket’s actual front closure in the edited frame, accounting for pose and occlusion, and compare the visible panel alignment with the source before concluding that it remains open. Keep complete closure distinct from partial progress, and return unknown when the closure cannot be reliably seen rather than treating obscured evidence as a confident failure. Do not change the rubric or force a yes from the reference label alone; the label constrains the aggregate, while the image evidence must support the node’s judgment.
s2: The repeated valid traces are not transport or dependency failures, but their confident “no progress” judgments may be over-relying on the edited jacket’s visible opening. Bind the comparison to the same front closure in both frames and assess whether the panels have moved together, accounting for the edited pose and drape: the source shows the jacket open, while the edited image shows it turned across her front, with the closure partly obscured. Distinguish visible partial progress from full closure, and use unknown if occlusion prevents a reliable comparison; do not infer either progress or its absence from pose alone. Preserve the existing criterion and do not use the aggregate reference label as atomic evidence.

response.content: {"text":"The node’s endpoint criterion is clear, but its binding is too narrow: it inspects only the edited frame and can mistake the jacket’s changed pose and drape for a clearly open closure. Bind the check to the same jacket and front-closure region across source and edit; account for the woman turning sideways and the panels being partly occluded. Assess visible panel alignment and any remaining opening, while distinguishing full closure from observable partial progress. If the closure’s extent cannot be judged, return unknown rather than a high-confidence fail. The repeated valid, queried traces indicate a visual-evidence/decision issue, not transport, schema, or dependency failure. Treat the reference label as an aggregate constraint, not atomic evidence, and do not force a pass or relax the full-closure requirement."}
